terms.grammar: conjunction: the indicative for a real condition, the present or perfect subjunctive for a supposed one, the imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive for one contrary to fact
evidence: Cato Agr. 1.7: sī mē rogābis, sīc dīcam
terms.comment: Where English puts a present after “if” for the future, Latin says the future or the future perfect: sī mē rogābis, if you ask me; sī … adjēcerit deus, if God grants (Sen. Ep. 12.9). Contrary to fact: the imperfect for the present (sī … concēderet, possem), the pluperfect for the past (sī … nātus esset). Sī mē amās, the “please” of Cicero’s letters.

terms.grammar: conjunction, with the moods of sī
evidence: Petr. 50.1: quod sī nōn frangerentur, māllem mihi quam aurum
terms.comment: Takes up what has just been said: “and if, but if”.

phrases.english: if you want to, you can
if you ask me, I shall say this

phrases.latin: crāstinum sī adjēcerit deus, laetī recipiāmus
phrases.english: if God adds a tomorrow, let us receive it gladly

phrases.latin: Bis est grātum quod opus est, ultrō sī offerās.
phrases.english: What is needed is twice welcome if you offer it unasked.

phrases.latin: sī mihi Nausicaa patriōs concēderet hortōs, Alcinoō possem dīcere “mālō meōs”
phrases.english: if Nausicaa offered me her father’s gardens, I could say to Alcinous: “I prefer my own”

phrases.latin: sī in Parthiā nātus esset, arcum īnfāns statim tenderet
phrases.english: had he been born in Parthia, he would have drawn a bow as a baby

phrases.latin: sed cūrā, sī mē amās, ut valeās
phrases.english: but please, take care of yourself
